question: Greek driving guides describe the category B theory test as how many questions?
explanation: The category B theory test is 30 multiple-choice questions drawn at random from the Ministry's question bank, answered on a computer.

question: How many wrong answers can you give on the Greek category B theory test and still pass?
explanation: Guides and Greek motoring press report a pass at 29 of 30 correct, so a second mistake fails the test. Check the current rule with your Transport Directorate.

question: Who keeps the question bank for the Greek theory test?
explanation: Law 4850/2021 sets up a theory test question bank run by the Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport; questions are drawn from it at random.

question: A candidate does not read Greek. How can they sit the theory test?
optionD: In a language the system offers
explanation: Law 4850/2021 makes the questionnaires available in foreign languages as well as in Greek, in Greek with audio and in Greek Sign Language.

question: From what age can a learner in Greece drive a car accompanied, after passing the tests?
explanation: Since Law 4850/2021, a 17-year-old who trains and passes the tests can drive accompanied on a provisional licence until turning 18.

question: At what age can you hold a full category B licence and drive alone in Greece?
explanation: A full category B licence is issued from 18. Younger successful candidates drive only accompanied, on a provisional licence.

question: A category B licence lets you drive a car with a maximum authorised mass of up to:
explanation: Category B covers vehicles up to 3,500 kg maximum authorised mass with no more than eight passenger seats besides the driver, under the EU licence rules Greece applies.

question: How many passenger seats, besides the driver's, may a category B vehicle have at most?
explanation: Category B covers vehicles with up to eight passenger seats plus the driver. A minibus with more seats needs a D1 or D licence.

question: What is the general blood alcohol limit for an experienced car driver in Greece?
explanation: The general limit is 0.5 grams of alcohol per litre of blood. A lower limit, 0.2 g/l, applies to novice and professional drivers and to riders.

question: A driver who passed the test 14 months ago may drive with a blood alcohol level of at most:
explanation: Greece sets 0.2 g/l for drivers in their first two years, for professional drivers and for motorcyclists and moped riders, against 0.5 g/l for other drivers.

question: Which of these drivers has the lower 0.2 g/l alcohol limit in Greece?
optionB: A driver with a hybrid car
optionD: A driver on a rural road
explanation: Professional drivers, novice drivers and riders of motorcycles and mopeds have the 0.2 g/l limit. Age, fuel type and road type do not change it.

question: Under the 2025 Highway Code, a driver caught above 1.1 g/l of alcohol faces:
explanation: Above 1.10 g/l, Article 46 of Law 5209/2025 makes it a criminal offence with at least two months' imprisonment, on top of a fine and losing the licence and registration for 180 days.

question: What does the KTEO certificate show for a car?
optionB: Its road tax has been paid
explanation: KTEO centres carry out the periodic technical inspection. The certificate and sticker show the car passed its roadworthiness test.

question: A car may only be driven on Greek roads if it has at least:
explanation: Third-party liability insurance is compulsory for every vehicle on the road. Comprehensive cover is optional.

question: Which document is the vehicle's registration certificate in Greece?
explanation: The άδεια κυκλοφορίας (registration certificate) belongs to the vehicle; the δίπλωμα οδήγησης is your driving licence.

question: Your licence has been withdrawn by the police for an offence. You may:
optionB: Drive in your own town only
optionC: Drive if a friend sits beside you
optionD: Not drive until it is returned
explanation: While a licence is withdrawn you have no right to drive any vehicle. Driving anyway is a separate, more serious offence.

question: Drugs or medicines that impair driving are:
explanation: Greek law forbids driving under the influence of any substance or medicine that impairs you, prescription or not. Read the leaflet and ask your doctor.

question: On a short trip across Athens, your rear-seat passenger says belts are only needed on highways. Is that right?
optionA: Yes, they are optional inside towns
optionB: No, belts are needed on all roads
explanation: Seat belts are compulsory in every seat that has one, on every road. Under the 2025 Code both an unbelted passenger and the driver can be fined.

question: Under the 2025 Highway Code, repeating the same serious offence within a set period leads to:
explanation: Law 5209/2025 brought in escalating penalties for repeat offences (υποτροπή): a second and third offence carry heavier fines and longer licence withdrawal.

question: Before taking the theory test for a first licence in Greece, a candidate normally:
explanation: Candidates register and take their theory training through a licensed driving school, which books them into the test at the Transport Directorate.

question: In Greece, danger warning signs (the K series) are usually:
explanation: Warning signs follow the Vienna Convention: a triangle, point up, with a red border and a black symbol on a white background.

question: A warning triangle shows a black line bending sharply to the left. It warns of:
optionD: A side road on the left
explanation: A single curve in a warning triangle shows a bend in the direction drawn. Slow down before the bend, not in it.

question: A warning triangle shows a line bending right, then left. It warns of:
explanation: Bend symbols are drawn as you will meet them: here the road turns right first, then left.

question: After the first autumn rain on a road near Patras, you pass a triangle with a skidding car drawn in it. It warns of:
explanation: The skid marks warn that the road can be slippery, especially after the first rain of autumn when oil and dust lift off the asphalt.

question: Approaching a village square, a red-bordered triangle shows a walking figure on zebra stripes. It warns of:
explanation: Be ready to stop for people on the crossing ahead. A ban on pedestrians would be a red-bordered circle instead.

question: A warning triangle shows two children, one leading the other. Where is it usually placed?
optionB: Near a school or play area
explanation: The children sign warns that children may be on or near the road. Slow down and expect sudden movements.

question: A warning triangle shows a worker with a shovel beside a heap. It warns of:
explanation: Expect workers, machines and narrowed lanes. Slow down and follow any temporary signs and signals.

question: A warning triangle shows a fence-like barrier. It warns of:
explanation: A gate or barrier symbol warns of a railway level crossing protected by barriers. A locomotive symbol means one without barriers.

question: On a country road near Larissa, a warning triangle shows an old steam engine. What is ahead?
explanation: With no barriers, you must look and listen both ways and cross only when no train is coming.

question: Before a level crossing you pass boards with three, then two, then one red diagonal stripe. The three-stripe board is:
explanation: The countdown boards tell you how close the crossing is: three stripes first, one stripe last and nearest, so you can judge your braking.

question: A warning triangle shows a slope rising to the right with "12%". It warns of:
explanation: The percentage gives the gradient. Change down in good time so the engine does not labour on the climb.

question: A steep descent warning triangle shows 12%. What does the 12% mean?
optionA: 12 km of slope ahead of you
explanation: The percentage is the gradient: the road drops 12 m for every 100 m travelled. Choose a lower gear before you start down.

question: Entering a mountain village, a warning triangle shows both road edges curving in towards each other. It warns of:
optionD: Two lanes merge at a toll
explanation: Both edges move in, so the carriageway gets narrower. Slow down and be ready to give way to oncoming traffic.

question: At the end of a dual carriageway, a warning triangle shows one arrow up and one arrow down side by side. It warns of:
explanation: You are leaving a one-way section or a dual carriageway. Expect oncoming traffic in the other lane.

question: A warning triangle shows a thick vertical line crossed by a thin horizontal one. It means:
optionD: A dead end, no way through
explanation: A thick line crossed by a thin one shows your road is the main road at the crossroads ahead. Still watch for drivers who pull out.

question: A warning triangle marks a crossroads of equal roads with no priority signs. At it you give way to:
explanation: Where no sign or signal gives priority, Greek rules give priority to the vehicle coming from the right.

question: Approaching the edge of a town in Crete, a warning triangle shows three curved arrows forming a circle. It warns of:
explanation: Slow down for a roundabout ahead and look for the sign at its entry that tells you who has priority.

question: Just past a blind bend, a warning triangle shows a set of three coloured lamps. It warns of:
explanation: Be ready to stop at signals that may be hidden by a bend or the brow of a hill.

question: A warning triangle shows rocks falling from a slope on the right. You should:
explanation: Common on Greek mountain roads. Watch for stones on the road and avoid stopping below the slope.

question: Driving through a forest on Mount Parnitha at dusk, you pass a warning triangle with a leaping deer. It warns of:
explanation: Wild animals may run onto the road, especially at dusk and at night. Slow down and be ready to stop.

question: On a rural road in Thessaly, a triangle with a red border shows a cow. It warns of:
explanation: Farm animals may be on or crossing the road. Pass slowly and do not sound the horn at them.

question: On a flat road near the Thessaloniki seafront, a red-bordered triangle shows a bicycle. It warns of:
explanation: Watch for cyclists at the place where a cycle track crosses or joins the road. A blue circle with a bicycle would be a compulsory cycle track.

question: A warning triangle shows a car beside water. It warns of:
explanation: The road leads to an unprotected quay or riverbank, common in Greek harbour towns. Slow down and watch the edge.

question: Before the Rio-Antirrio bridge approach, a warning triangle shows a windsock blown out to one side. It warns of:
explanation: Strong crosswinds can push the car sideways, especially on bridges and exposed coastal roads. Hold the wheel firmly and slow down.

question: A warning triangle shows a bumpy road surface. It warns of:
explanation: The road surface ahead is uneven. Slow down so the car stays stable and under control.

question: A warning triangle with an exclamation mark and a plate below means:
optionD: A sign that is out of use
explanation: The exclamation mark warns of a danger with no symbol of its own. The plate below says what it is.

question: A side street meets the main road under an eight-sided red sign reading STOP. You must:
explanation: At a STOP sign you must come to a full stop at the line even if the road looks clear, then give way to traffic on the main road.

question: At a side road you face a red-bordered triangle standing on its point, with nothing inside. It means:
explanation: Slow down and stop if needed to give way to traffic on the road you are joining. You need not stop if it is clear.

question: How long does the yellow diamond with a white border keep you on a priority road?
explanation: This sign shows a priority road: drivers joining from side roads must give way to you at each junction until the end-of-priority sign.

question: After the end-of-priority sign (the yellow diamond with black lines), which rule applies at an unsigned junction?
explanation: From the end sign your road no longer has priority, so give way to traffic from the right at junctions unless signs say otherwise.

question: Before a narrow bridge, a round red-bordered sign shows two arrows pointing opposite ways; the arrow pointing up, in your direction of travel, is red. It means:
explanation: At the narrow section you must give way to oncoming vehicles: the red arrow marks the traffic that gives way, and here it is yours.

question: A lane into an old town square is marked by a round sign: white inside, red rim, no symbol or number. It means:
explanation: A plain red-bordered circle closes the road to all vehicles in both directions. Pedestrians may still use it.

question: You want a short cut through a street whose entrance shows a solid red disc with a white bar. What should you do?
optionD: Enter only at night, with care
explanation: No entry for vehicles from this side, often at the exit end of a one-way street.

question: On a winding road above Delphi, a round red-rimmed sign shows a red car beside a black car. It tells you:
explanation: You must not overtake motor vehicles with more than two wheels until the end-of-restriction sign.

question: Past a red-bordered circle showing 50, your speedometer reads 58 km/h. What should you do?
explanation: A number in a red-bordered circle is a maximum speed. A minimum speed is shown as a number in a blue circle.

question: A blue circle with "30" in white means:
explanation: A blue circle gives an order. With a number it is the lowest speed you may drive, unless traffic or conditions prevent it.

question: Outside a bakery, a sign has a blue disc, a red rim and a single red slash. It means:
explanation: One stripe forbids parking; you may still stop briefly to set down or pick up passengers. Two crossed stripes forbid stopping too.

question: Under a no-stopping sign (blue disc, red rim, red X), when may you still stop?
explanation: Two crossed stripes forbid stopping and parking alike, except where traffic forces you to stop.

question: Which sign forbids turning left at the next junction?
optionB: Blue disc with a left arrow
optionD: Blue square with a left-pointing arrow
explanation: A crossed-out arrow in a red ring forbids the turn shown. A blue disc with an arrow orders you to go that way, and a triangle warns of a bend.

question: In the middle of a busy avenue, a round red-rimmed sign shows a hooked arrow turning back on itself, with a red bar through it. It means:
explanation: U-turns are banned here. Use a roundabout or a place where turning is safe and allowed.

question: A red-bordered circle with a horn crossed through means:
explanation: You may not sound the horn here, except to avoid immediate danger.

question: A red-bordered circle with "3.5 t" means:
explanation: Vehicles whose laden weight exceeds the figure may not enter. A car is well under this limit.

question: A red-bordered circle with "2.8 m" between two arrows pointing at each other vertically means:
explanation: Vertical arrows show the maximum height of a vehicle, including any load or roof box. Horizontal arrows would be a width limit.

question: Just before a junction, a round blue sign carries a white arrow bent to the right. It means:
explanation: A blue circle gives an order: you must turn right at this point.

question: On a traffic island, a round blue sign has a white arrow slanting down to the right. It means:
explanation: Keep to the right of the island or obstruction marked by the sign.

question: At the entry to a junction, a round blue sign shows three white arrows circling anticlockwise. It tells you:
explanation: In right-hand traffic you travel round a roundabout anticlockwise. Who gives way at entry depends on the signs there.

question: On the seafront in Thessaloniki, a round blue sign with a white bicycle marks a track. May you park on the track briefly?
explanation: The track is for cyclists, and cyclists must use it. Drivers may not drive or park on it.

question: A red-bordered circle with "50", crossed by grey diagonal lines, means:
explanation: Grey diagonal lines cancel the limit shown. The general limit for that type of road then applies.

question: You pass a white disc with grey diagonal lines and no number. Which ban does it not end?
explanation: This sign ends every prohibition previously signed for moving vehicles, such as speed limits and no-overtaking. Parking bans are separate and continue.

question: A red-bordered circle shows a walking figure. Which road user is it aimed at?
explanation: Pedestrians may not use this road, often on expressways and in tunnels.

question: A rectangular blue sign with a white "P" and a plate showing a wheelchair means:
explanation: The plate limits the parking space to vehicles of people with disabilities who hold the permit. Others may not park there.

question: A red-bordered circle with a lorry, and a plate reading 3.5 t, stands at a village entrance. May you drive your car in?
optionA: No, it bans every vehicle there
optionB: Yes, the ban is for lorries
explanation: Goods vehicles above the weight on the plate may not enter. Cars may pass.

question: In Greece, direction signs with a green background lead to:
explanation: Green direction signs point to motorways (αυτοκινητόδρομοι); blue ones are used on other main roads. Brown signs point to sights.

question: A brown direction sign with a white symbol usually points to:
explanation: Brown signs guide drivers to cultural and tourist sites, very common for Greece's ancient sites and monasteries.

question: Near Delphi, a brown sign shows a temple. What kind of place does it point to?
explanation: Brown signs direct you to tourist, cultural and archaeological sites.

question: A blue square sign with a white T shape, the top bar red, means:
explanation: This is the dead-end sign (αδιέξοδο): the road ahead leads nowhere, so you will need to turn round.

question: At a Piraeus street corner, a rectangular blue plate shows a white arrow. Traffic in that street may move:
optionB: In both directions at all times
explanation: A rectangular sign with a straight arrow shows the street is one-way in the arrow's direction. A round blue sign would be an order to go that way.

question: Near a hospital in Larissa, a blue sign with a hospital bed symbol stands beside the road. How should you drive past?
optionA: Sounding the horn to warn the staff
optionC: Faster, to keep the road clear
optionD: In the bus lane, out of the way
explanation: This sign marks a nearby hospital. Avoid unnecessary noise and watch for ambulances entering or leaving.

question: At Greek traffic lights, which light comes after steady amber?
explanation: The sequence is green, amber, red. Amber means stop at the line unless you are so close that stopping suddenly would be dangerous.

question: A traffic light shows red and you are at the line. You may move off when:
explanation: Red means stop until green shows. Even on green, move off only once the junction is clear of crossing traffic and pedestrians.

question: A traffic light flashes amber continuously. It means:
explanation: A flashing amber light means the signals are not controlling traffic. Slow down and follow the signs and the normal priority rules.

question: At Athens lights, a green arrow pointing right sits below the red light but is not lit. May you turn right?
explanation: A filter arrow lets you go only while it is lit. Until then the red light applies to every direction.

question: A traffic police officer faces you with an arm raised straight up. You should:
explanation: An officer's raised arm means all traffic must stop, except vehicles already in the junction that cannot stop safely.

question: A traffic police officer stands side-on to you with arms stretched out. You may:
explanation: With the officer side-on, traffic moving in the line of the arms may go; traffic facing the chest or back must stop.

question: A traffic officer's signal conflicts with a green traffic light. You obey:
explanation: Signals from a police officer override traffic lights, signs and markings.

question: On a coastal road the centre line is solid white for a long stretch. You must:
explanation: A solid line may not be crossed. Overtaking that would need you to cross it is not allowed.

question: The solid centre line gives way to a dashed white one on a straight stretch. Now:
optionC: You may cross it if safe
explanation: A broken line separates traffic and can be crossed, for example to overtake, when it is safe and allowed.

question: A double centre line has a solid line on your side and a broken line on the far side. Crossing it from your lane is:
explanation: With double lines, only drivers on the side of the broken line may cross. The solid line on your side forbids it.

question: A wide unbroken white bar is painted across your lane where you meet a junction. It is:
explanation: A solid transverse line marks where to stop for a STOP sign, a red light or an officer's signal.

question: A transverse line of short white dashes at a junction marks:
explanation: Dashed transverse lines go with a give-way sign: wait behind them if you need to give way.

question: Why must you not overtake a car that is slowing down for a pedestrian crossing?
optionA: It may be about to turn right
explanation: A car slowing for a crossing can hide someone stepping out in front of it. Never overtake on or near a pedestrian crossing.

question: White diagonal stripes in a striped area bordered by a solid line mean:
explanation: Hatched areas separate lanes or protect turning traffic. Do not drive or park on them.

question: A painted arrow in your lane points left. It means:
explanation: Arrows on the road show where each lane goes. Choose your lane early and follow its arrow.

question: Yellow kerb markings in Greek towns are often painted next to:
explanation: Yellow kerb markings show where stopping and parking are not allowed, for example at bus stops and in front of fire hydrants.

question: Temporary yellow lines painted at roadworks conflict with the white lines. You follow:
explanation: At roadworks, temporary yellow markings override the permanent white ones.

question: A bus lane is marked with a wide line and the word ΛΕΩΦΟΡΕΙΑ or BUS. Your car may:
optionC: Use it when it is empty
explanation: Bus lanes are for buses and other vehicles shown on the signs. Driving or parking a private car in one is an offence.

question: Driving into a holiday town, you see a blue sign with a white bed on it. It points to:
explanation: The bed symbol points to accommodation. A tent symbol would be a campsite and an H a hospital.

question: A blue sign shows a white fuel pump. It means:
explanation: The fuel pump marks a filling station. Electric chargers have their own symbol showing a plug.

question: At a crossroads in a Cretan village with no signs or lights, a car arrives on your right at the same time as you. Who goes first?
optionB: You, as it is on the right
explanation: The general rule of the Greek Highway Code is priority from the right wherever signs, signals or an officer do not say otherwise.

question: You arrive at a roundabout with a give way sign at its entry. You give way to:
explanation: With a give way or STOP sign at the entry, vehicles already circulating have priority. Many Greek roundabouts are signed this way.

question: In Greece, who decides who has priority at a roundabout?
explanation: The Highway Code leaves priority at each roundabout to its signs. With a give way sign at the entry, circulating traffic goes first; with no signs, priority from the right applies.

question: A roundabout has no signs at all. Under the priority-from-the-right rule, the vehicle with priority is:
optionD: The one joining from the right
explanation: Without signs, the general rule applies, so a vehicle joining from the right goes first. Greek motoring guides warn this differs from most of Europe.

question: You are on a road with a yellow diamond priority sign. A car waits in a side road on your right. Who goes first?
explanation: The priority road sign overrides priority from the right: drivers in side roads must give way to you. Still be ready if they pull out.

question: You signal to turn left off an avenue. A car coming the other way is heading straight across. You:
explanation: Turning left across oncoming traffic, you wait until vehicles going straight on or turning right have passed.

question: You are turning right into a side street. A pedestrian is crossing that street. You:
explanation: When you turn, you must give way to pedestrians crossing the road you are turning into.

question: On Kifisias Avenue an ambulance closes on you with blue lights and siren. You:
optionD: Pull over to let it pass
explanation: Emergency vehicles using lights and siren have priority. Move aside safely and give them room; never block a junction to do so.

question: At an unsignalled junction you meet a tram. Generally you:
explanation: Article 30 of the 2025 Code gives trams priority, and they run on fixed rails and cannot swerve. Give way to them unless signals say otherwise.

question: Leaving a beach car park onto the coast road, you must cross a cycle path. A cyclist is coming along it. Who goes first?
explanation: Leaving a car park, driveway or petrol station, you give way to everyone on the road, including cyclists on a cycle path and pedestrians on the pavement.

question: You are joining a main road from an unmade dirt track. You:
optionB: Go first if you are right
optionC: Give way to the main road
explanation: Article 30 of the 2025 Code makes drivers coming from an unpaved road, a driveway, a car park or a filling station give way to traffic on the road.

question: Two cars meet on a narrow mountain road where only one can pass. Who normally gives way?
explanation: Article 22 of the 2025 Code makes the vehicle going down give way on a steep narrow road, because starting again uphill is harder. Exceptions exist, for example for buses and heavier vehicles.

question: Why must you not enter a junction on green when you cannot get across it?
explanation: Never enter a junction unless you can clear it; otherwise you block cross traffic when the lights change.

question: Barriers at a level crossing are coming down and red lights flash. You:
optionD: Cross if no train is in sight
explanation: Once the lights flash or the barriers start to move you must stop. Wait until the barriers are fully up and the lights stop.

question: You stall on a level crossing and cannot restart. Your first step is to:
optionB: Wait for help in the car
optionD: Push the car with passengers inside
explanation: Get everyone out and away from the track first, then warn the railway or call 112. A car can be replaced; people cannot.

question: At a level crossing without barriers or lights, you should:
optionC: Follow the car in front closely
explanation: With no protection, you are the only safety system. Slow down, look and listen in both directions, then cross without stopping on the track.

question: A school bus has stopped at the roadside in a village and children are getting off. You are behind it. What is the main risk?
optionA: A child stepping out from it
optionD: Its door swinging out into your lane
explanation: Children may cross in front of or behind the bus without looking. Pass slowly, ready to stop.

question: A bus in a built-up area signals to pull out from a stop. You should:
explanation: Help buses leave stops in towns where you can do so safely, by slowing down and letting them move out.

question: Two cars arrive at a crossroads at the same time from opposite directions, one turning left. Who goes first?
optionB: The car on the bigger road
optionD: The first to flash its lights
explanation: A driver turning left gives way to oncoming traffic going straight on or turning right.

question: Who has priority on a zebra crossing without traffic lights in Greece?
explanation: Pedestrians on a zebra crossing have priority. Stop before the crossing and wait until they are safely across.

question: At a junction controlled by lights that are not working, you follow:
optionD: Your own sense of right of way
explanation: If the lights are out or flashing amber, the priority signs at the junction apply, and where there are none, priority from the right.

question: A STOP sign and a traffic light at the same junction disagree. The light is green. You:
explanation: Working traffic lights override priority signs. The signs apply only when the lights are off or flashing amber.

question: At a crossroads you have a STOP sign and the other road has none. You must:
optionA: Give way to the right only
optionB: Give way to the left only
explanation: A STOP sign takes away your priority on both sides. Stop, then go only when the main road is clear.

question: You are on a roundabout with several lanes and want the second exit. Before leaving you:
optionA: Cut across lanes at the exit
optionB: Stop in the lane and wait
optionC: Signal left all the way round
explanation: In right-hand traffic you leave a roundabout to the right. Move to the outer lane in good time and signal right just before your exit.

question: An approaching car flashes its headlights at you at a junction. This means:
explanation: Flashing headlights only signal that the driver is there. Never treat it as permission; make sure the way is clear yourself.

question: You meet a funeral procession or a column of soldiers on foot. You should:
explanation: Organised processions and columns must not be broken up. Wait or pass carefully only where it is safe and allowed.

question: Under the 2025 Highway Code, the general car limit on a single-lane street in a built-up area, with no sign, is:
explanation: Article 24 of Law 5209/2025 cut the general built-up limit to 30 km/h, in force since 1 January 2026, unless signs set another figure. Some multi-lane town roads keep 50 km/h.

question: In a built-up area, a one-way street with two marked lanes and no speed sign has a car limit of:
explanation: Article 24 of the 2025 Code keeps 50 km/h on one-way streets with at least two marked lanes in towns, unless a sign says otherwise; most other town streets drop to 30 km/h.

question: Outside built-up areas, on an ordinary road with no sign, the car limit is:
explanation: The general limit for cars on roads outside built-up areas is 90 km/h, unless the road is an expressway or a motorway or signs say otherwise.

question: On a Greek motorway (αυτοκινητόδρομος), the general limit for a car without a trailer is:
explanation: Cars may do up to 130 km/h on motorways unless signs set a lower limit, for example near toll stations or roadworks.

question: On an expressway (οδός ταχείας κυκλοφορίας), the general limit for a car is:
explanation: Expressways, roads built for fast traffic but not full motorways, have a car limit of 110 km/h unless signs say otherwise.

question: A speed limit is the most you may drive. The right speed is:
explanation: Adapt your speed to the road, weather, traffic and your own view ahead. In rain or fog the safe speed is often well below the limit.

question: You must always be able to stop:
optionB: Within the length of your car
optionC: In the distance you can see clear
explanation: Drive at a speed that lets you stop within the stretch of road you can see is clear, especially at bends and hill crests.

question: On a dry road, a simple way to keep a safe gap from the car ahead is to leave at least:
explanation: Count two seconds after the car ahead passes a fixed point. Double the gap or more on wet roads.

question: Your reaction distance is 15 m and your braking distance is 25 m. What is your stopping distance?
explanation: Stopping distance is the distance travelled while you react plus the distance the car takes to stop once you brake: 15 + 25 = 40 m.

question: You brake from 80 km/h instead of 40 km/h on the same dry road. Your braking distance is about:
explanation: Braking distance grows with the square of the speed, so twice the speed needs about four times the distance to stop.

question: On a wet road, compared with a dry one, your braking distance is:
explanation: Water reduces grip, so the car takes much further to stop. Leave a far larger gap and brake gently.

question: Driving on the right in Greece, you catch up with a slow tractor on an open road. Once it is safe, you pass it:
explanation: In right-hand traffic you overtake on the left. The exception is a vehicle signalling and positioned to turn left, which you pass on its right.

question: A car ahead signals left and moves to the centre of the road to turn. You may pass it:
explanation: When a vehicle has clearly moved over to turn left, you may pass it on the right if there is room and it is safe.

question: Before overtaking, you must first make sure that:
optionA: The driver ahead waves you on
optionB: No one behind is overtaking you
explanation: Check your mirrors and blind spot. If a vehicle behind has already begun to overtake you, you must wait.

question: Overtaking is not allowed:
optionB: On a road with a broken line
explanation: You must not overtake at or approaching a pedestrian crossing, at junctions, at level crossings, near hill crests or on bends with poor view.

question: A car is overtaking you on a narrow road when an oncoming lorry appears. What should you do?
optionC: Flash your lights to warn it off
optionD: Ease off to let it back in
explanation: Hold your speed or ease off so the overtaking driver can pull back in. Speeding up is dangerous and forbidden.

question: Approaching a hill crest where you cannot see oncoming traffic, you:
optionD: May overtake if the road is wide
explanation: Never overtake where you cannot see that the road ahead is clear for long enough to pass and pull back in.

question: On a multi-lane road outside towns, you should normally drive in:
explanation: Keep to the right-hand lane and use the others to overtake, returning to the right once you have passed.

question: On a three-lane avenue you decide to move one lane to the left. What is the right sequence?
explanation: Check mirrors and blind spot, signal in good time, check again, then move over smoothly if it is safe.

question: Why should you never drive in another vehicle's blind spot for long?
explanation: In the blind spot you are hidden from the other driver's mirrors. Drop back or pass so you can be seen.

question: Driving very slowly without reason on an open road is:
optionA: Not allowed if it holds others up
explanation: Driving so slowly that you hold up traffic without good reason is not allowed and can lead to risky overtakes behind you.

question: You plan to do a U-turn. Where is it never allowed?
explanation: U-turns are banned on motorways and expressways, on bends, near hill crests and wherever signs forbid them.

question: Reversing for a long distance on a main road is:
explanation: Reverse only for short distances where you need to, such as parking, and never on motorways.

question: An electric scooter (e-scooter) on the road may travel at most at:
explanation: The 2025 Highway Code sets 25 km/h for electric personal mobility vehicles and bars them from roads whose car limit is above 50 km/h.

question: The road ahead is wet and covered with fallen leaves. You should:
explanation: Wet leaves are very slippery. Reduce speed early so you need no sharp braking or steering.

question: A sign shows "80" on a road where the general limit would be 90 km/h. You must drive at:
explanation: A posted limit replaces the general one for that stretch until another sign changes it.

question: In a two-way street in Greece, you normally park:
optionD: In the middle of the road
explanation: Park on the right-hand side, in the direction of traffic, unless signs allow otherwise. In one-way streets either side may be allowed.

question: Where is parking never allowed?
explanation: Never stop or park on a pedestrian crossing, on a cycle track, at a bus stop or where you block a junction or a driveway.

question: Parking on the pavement is:
explanation: Pavements are for pedestrians, wheelchairs and pushchairs. Park there only where bays are marked for it.

question: You may stop briefly to let a passenger out, but not park, under which sign?
optionA: Blue circle with a red X
explanation: The one-stripe sign forbids parking but allows a short stop. The red X forbids stopping too.

question: You have parked on a street with a cycle lane beside it. Before opening your door you:
explanation: Look in the mirror and over your shoulder. A door opened into a cyclist's path can cause a serious crash.

question: You park facing downhill on a steep Athens street with a kerb. Which pair of actions holds the car best?
explanation: Turned towards the kerb, the wheels catch on it if the car rolls. Apply the parking brake firmly as well, and leave a manual car in gear.

question: When leaving a parked car, you must:
explanation: Switch off the engine, apply the parking brake and lock the car so it cannot roll away or be taken.

question: Parking in front of an entrance to a fire station or garage is:
optionB: Allowed if you stay in the car
explanation: Blocking entrances, especially those emergency vehicles use, is forbidden at all times.

question: A parking space has a blue sign with a wheelchair symbol. You may park there:
optionB: If the car park is full
explanation: These spaces are for people with disabilities who hold the special permit. Using one without it is an offence.

question: You see a cyclist ahead on a narrow road. When overtaking, you should:
explanation: Cyclists may wobble or swerve round potholes. Wait until you can give them wide space, then pass.

question: At a bus stop in Patras, a pedestrian with a white cane stands near the kerb. Why should you avoid sounding your horn?
optionA: It is banned at all bus stops
optionC: It can startle or confuse them
explanation: A white cane shows the person is blind or partly sighted. Give them time and do not use the horn, which can startle them.

question: You drive along a Greek village street lined with houses and parked cars at school closing time. What is the safest speed?
optionD: Slow enough to stop at once
explanation: Children can run into the road from between parked cars without warning. Drive slowly enough to stop at once.

question: You follow a moped rider on a gravel patch. You should:
explanation: Two-wheelers can lose grip on gravel or wet surfaces. Give them extra room in case they fall.

question: A horse rider is on the road ahead. You should:
explanation: Noise can frighten horses. Slow down, pass wide and quietly, and be ready to stop.

question: A street is signed as a residential zone, where pedestrians may use its whole width. You should drive:
optionC: Very slowly, letting walkers go first
optionD: At 50 km/h when it is empty
explanation: In a residential or traffic-calmed zone pedestrians and children may be anywhere in the street. Drive very slowly and let them go first.

question: Where may you use the horn in a built-up area?
explanation: In towns the horn is only for avoiding danger. At night, flash your headlights instead.

question: On a road with no pavement, pedestrians should walk:
explanation: Walking on the left facing traffic lets pedestrians see what is coming. Drivers should expect them there and give them room.

question: Why should you avoid parking on a steep hill with the parking brake alone in a manual car?
optionB: It could slip and let it roll
explanation: A parking brake can slip on a steep slope. Leave a manual car in gear as well and turn the wheels so the car would roll away from traffic.

question: A bus is stopped at a stop with no bay. Passengers are getting off. You should:
explanation: Passengers may cross in front of the bus. Pass slowly with room, or wait if the road is narrow.

question: Driving or parking in a cycle lane is:
explanation: Cycle lanes and tracks are for cyclists. Driving or stopping in them puts riders into traffic.

question: A child shorter than 1.35 m travels in your car. The child must use:
explanation: Under the EU rules applied in Greece, children under 1.35 m (and under 12) must ride in a child seat or booster suited to their size and weight.

question: A rear-facing baby seat may go in the front passenger seat only if:
optionD: The trip is a short one
explanation: An inflating airbag can strike a rear-facing seat with great force. Switch the airbag off or put the seat in the back.

question: Which phone set-up is legal for a Greek driver making a call on the move?
explanation: Holding a phone while driving is banned; a hands-free kit is allowed. The 2025 Code raised the penalties and makes them heavier each time the offence is repeated.

question: On a long drive to Thessaloniki you realise you cannot remember the last few kilometres. What should you do?
optionB: Open the window and go on
explanation: Missing stretches of road you have just driven is a sign of tiredness. Only rest cures it, so stop somewhere safe and take a break or a short nap.

question: When should you check the car's tyre pressures?
explanation: Check about every two weeks and before long trips, when the tyres are cold, using the figures in the car's handbook.

question: Before a summer trip to the Peloponnese you check your tyres. The legal minimum tread depth for a car in Greece is:
explanation: Car tyres need at least 1.6 mm of tread across the central part. Grip in the wet drops sharply well before that.

question: Which items must a car in Greece carry?
optionA: Spare bulbs and a tow rope
explanation: Greek rules require a warning triangle, a first aid kit and a fire extinguisher in every car.

question: A smooth, economical way to drive is to:
explanation: Looking well ahead, changing up early and easing off instead of braking saves fuel and lowers emissions.

question: Why should the head restraint be set high and close to the back of your head?
optionA: To reduce whiplash in a crash
optionC: To improve your view to the rear
explanation: A head restraint set high and close to the head protects against whiplash in a rear impact.

question: The red oil can light comes on as you drive on the motorway. What is the risk if you carry on?
optionD: An empty fuel tank very soon
explanation: Low oil pressure can wreck the engine within minutes. Stop where safe, switch off and check the oil level.

question: The steering feels heavy and the car pulls to one side. The likely cause is:
explanation: Low pressure in a front tyre makes the steering heavy and pulls the car to that side. Stop and check.

question: Driving with under-inflated tyres causes:
explanation: Soft tyres flex more, use more fuel, wear faster and make the car less stable in bends and braking.

question: You drive your nephew, aged 10, to school in Volos. Who must make sure he is properly restrained?
explanation: The driver must make sure children are properly restrained. Under the 2025 Code an unbelted passenger can also mean a fine for the driver.

question: Your ABS warning light stays on. Your normal brakes:
explanation: The ordinary brakes still work, but wheels may lock in hard braking. Have the system checked soon.

question: Which number reaches emergency services from any phone in Greece and across the EU?
explanation: 112 works everywhere in the EU, free, even from a phone with no SIM credit. Greece also has its own numbers, such as 100 for the police.

question: Your engine dies on the Athens to Thessaloniki motorway. Where do you bring the car to rest?
explanation: Get as far right as possible, onto the emergency lane (ΛΕΑ), switch on hazard lights and put on a reflective vest if you have one.

question: After a breakdown on a motorway hard shoulder, passengers should wait:
optionA: In the car with belts on
optionB: Beside the car on the road
explanation: Cars on the hard shoulder are often hit by passing traffic. Get everyone out on the side away from the traffic and behind the barrier.

question: Driving along the motorway emergency lane (ΛΕΑ) to skip a queue is:
explanation: The emergency lane is kept clear for breakdowns and emergency vehicles. Driving in it is a serious offence.

question: You have broken down on an ordinary road. You place the warning triangle:
optionC: Right in front of the car
explanation: Put the triangle far enough behind your car that drivers see it in time to slow down, further on fast roads and before bends.

question: In which case is it right to switch on hazard warning lights?
explanation: Hazard lights warn others that your stopped vehicle is a danger, or briefly that traffic ahead has stopped suddenly on a fast road.

question: You come across a crash where people are hurt. Your first action is to:
explanation: Stop safely, switch on hazards and warn other traffic, then call 112. Move injured people only if they are in immediate danger.

question: Your car touches another at a junction in Heraklion. Under the law, every driver involved must:
optionA: Drive on if no one is hurt
explanation: Every driver involved must stop, help the injured, and exchange details. If anyone is hurt, call the police and stay at the scene.

question: Two cars collide with only damage and no injuries. The drivers can record it on:
explanation: The European accident statement (φιλικός διακανονισμός) lets drivers record a minor crash together for the insurers. It is not an admission of fault.

question: When should you switch from main beam to dipped beam as an oncoming car approaches at night?
explanation: Dip your lights in good time when you meet or follow other vehicles so you do not dazzle their drivers. Use main beam only when no one is ahead.

question: A car coming towards you at night dazzles you with main beam. You should:
explanation: Look towards the right-hand edge of the road and slow down, ready to stop, until your eyes recover.

question: In thick fog with visibility under 50 m, you may use:
explanation: Use dipped beam and fog lights in thick fog. Main beam reflects off the fog and makes it harder to see.

question: Driving into a tunnel in daylight, you should:
explanation: Dipped headlights are needed in tunnels so you see and are seen. Take off sunglasses too.

question: After a storm on the Egnatia Odos, the steering suddenly feels light as you hit standing water. You should:
explanation: Lift off the accelerator gently and keep the steering straight until the tyres grip again. Hard braking or steering can spin the car.

question: A flash flood has covered the road ahead and you cannot see the surface. You should:
explanation: Floodwater can hide washed-out road and sweep a car away even at modest depth. Turn back and find another route.

question: On a snowy mountain road, which is the best way to drive?
explanation: Smooth inputs and a higher gear reduce wheel spin. Carry snow chains where signs require them and know how to fit them.
